transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Emily Rogers (Verdant Head of ML), Diego Martinez (Platform Eng), Nina Lowe (Product)
Recording note: auto-transcript, some errors expected

Auto-summary (optional):
- Purpose: scope a 6-week pilot to validate unit economics and perf for Verdant's query workload.
- Success criteria discussed: latency SLOs, per-token cost targets, throughput targets, and data controls.
- Agreed next steps: share sample data, run baseline benchmarks, exchange pricing and security docs.

Topics covered:
1) Workload characterization: sequence lengths, qps patterns, batched vs interactive routes
2) Cost model: per-token math, batching and cache impact, quantization tradeoffs
3) Benchmark plan & timeline: baseline, optimization, report cadence
4) Security/compliance gating and pilot contract items

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making the time. Intro from Redwood side real quick, I'm Avery, I'll own the pilot contract and pricing, Marcus is our SE who will run the perf harness.
[00:12] Emily Rogers: Thanks, Avery. Hi Marcus, hi all. Quick context — Verdant runs a mixture of short transactional queries (~8-40 tokens) and longer assistant-style flows (~300-1200 tokens) for a subset of customers. We're trying to validate production economics before we commit to dedicated infra.
[00:28] Marcus Patel: Got it. Two obvious axes: (1) average sequence distribution and peak qps, (2) how tolerant you are to tail latency. That determines batching knob and whether caching helps.
[00:40] Diego Martinez: For peaks we see spikes to ~120 qps for the conversational route but average is ~15 qps. For transactional APIs it's very spiky, short payloads.
[00:55] Nina Lowe: And budget-wise we have an internal target — keep marginal cost under $0.50 per 1k requests for the most common route, which corresponds to about X tokens — we need help mapping tokens to per-request cost.
[01:10] Marcus Patel: Okay that's useful. We'll need sample logs to translate request counts to tokens. Also important: do you have any SLOs for 95th or 99th latency?
[01:20] Emily Rogers: We want 95th < 150ms for transactional, and 95th < 800ms for long assistant flows. If those are unrealistic at reasonable cost we can re-evaluate.
[01:31] Avery Chen: Good constraints. From a Redwood POV the knobs we tune are: batch size and max_wait_ms, prefix/KV cache for repeated context, async streaming for user-facing latency, and model quantization (int8, 4-bit). Those change per-token cost and tail.
[01:47] Marcus Patel: I'll note some initial hypotheses: for short tokens, small batch size with aggressive batching latency (20ms) gets cost savings without blowing 95th; for long sequences batching helps less per token but can amortize overhead. Prefix caching can dramatically cut repeated token generation when you have repetition across sessions.
[02:05] Diego Martinez: Are there numbers you can give us now? Ballpark per-token costs for, say, a 13B model in int8 vs 4-bit on dedicated vs hosted?
[02:15] Avery Chen: Ballpark — hosted (shared) for a 13B-ish quantized model might be around $0.6–$1.2 per 1k tokens depending on ROI and caching. Dedicated can push that down maybe 30–50% with reserved nodes and larger batch windows. 4-bit usually reduces cost another 10–20% vs int8 but depends on perf reg.
[02:33] Emily Rogers: That's a wide range. Can we tie it to concrete runs? Our CFO wants per-1M token price so they can model ARR impact.
[02:42] Marcus Patel: Absolutely. We'll run a 1M-token baseline on your sample with two quant profiles (int8, 4-bit) and two batch configs (low-latency batch target vs high-throughput batch) and report token throughput, p95 latency, and cost estimate. That will give you a per-1M token number for the exact workload.
[02:58] Nina Lowe: How long to run that?
[03:01] Marcus Patel: With your sample and our harness, each run is about 1–2 hours. We'll do a matrix of 4 runs for initial baseline, then one or two optimization passes. So estimate 6–8hrs of SE time across a few days.
[03:14] Emily Rogers: Ok good. On security: we need SOC2 docs, KMS integration capability (customer managed keys), and a VPC/private option for the pilot if possible.
[03:25] Avery Chen: We'll include SOC2 and ISO docs. For the pilot you can choose hosted or dedicated; if you need VPC peering for data egress controls, Redwood Private is an option but that pushes timeline a bit. We can do hosted with strict retention and KMS first.
[03:40] Diego Martinez: For our procurement team, they'll also want to see egress controls and audit logs at token level if possible.
[03:46] Avery Chen: We have token-level cost/latency breakdowns and per-route traces in the Console; audit logs can be exported. We'll put links in the security pack.
[03:56] Nina Lowe: Back to success criteria — besides latency thresholds and cost targets, we also want generation quality not to regress more than a 5% drop on our internal eval. How do we measure quality in the pilot?
[04:07] Marcus Patel: Typical approach: we take your eval set (a few hundred prompts with ground-truth or acceptable output criteria) and run automated metrics — exact-match or embedding-based similarity — plus a small human spot-check. We'll include regression alerts and compare model variants.
[04:22] Emily Rogers: We'll share an eval set. Note: some prompts contain PII so we'll need NDAs or redaction.
[04:28] Avery Chen: We can do a redacted sample as first step; SE will mark fields that need special handling. We'll include an NDA template if needed.
[04:35] 
[06:12] (transcript jump — mid-discussion paraphrased)
[06:12] Marcus Patel: On the batching knobs: two main settings — target batch size (or target tokens per batch) and max_wait_ms. For interactive UX we often set max_wait_ms low (10–30ms) and batch size small. For backend jobs you can push max_wait_ms to 100–200ms and saturate larger batches. The effective per-token GPU time goes down with larger batches because of kernel amortization.
[06:36] Diego Martinez: What's the common sweet spot for mixed workloads? We have 70% transactional short, 30% long, plus spikes.
[06:44] Marcus Patel: For mixed, a multi-route strategy usually wins: route short low-latency traffic to a small batch config and long flows to a separate pool tuned for throughput. Smart routing reduces cost without impacting p95 for critical paths.
[06:59] Avery Chen: Also prefix/KV caching can reduce tokens generated for assistant flows if you reuse system prompts or boilerplate context across users. That can be a big delta for per-token cost.
[07:10] Emily Rogers: Do you support prefix caching out-of-the-box? How much savings should we expect?
[07:15] Marcus Patel: Yes. If you have repeated 100-token system prompts across sessions, and 60% of them are identical, you could cut generated tokens by up to that repetition fraction for the cached prefix. For our customers we've seen effective token reductions of 10–35% depending on reuse.
[07:32] Nina Lowe: About quantization: is there a noticeable quality delta from int8 -> 4-bit? Some of our prompts are sensitive to small wording changes.
[07:39] Marcus Patel: It varies by model and prompt. For many models 4-bit is perceptually similar but you must validate on your eval set; sometimes you see edge-case regressions. That's why the pilot matrix includes both quant profiles.
[07:51] Emily Rogers: Ok, timeline question — we have a board review in early April. What's a realistic pilot timeline to deliver hard numbers before then?
[07:59] Avery Chen: If we start this week, here's a possible cadence: Week 0 (this week): share samples + NDA; Week 1: SE runs baseline 1M-token matrix and delivers initial per-1M-token numbers; Week 2: tuning (batching, caching) + focused runs; Week 3: run quality evals and spot human checks; Week 4: compile final pilot report and pricing; Week 5: exec review and follow-ups. That's a 4–5 week timeline to get board-ready numbers.
[08:26] Diego Martinez: That should work for us. We just need the baseline numbers with cost per 1M tokens and a table showing sensitivity (batch size, quant).
[08:34] Marcus Patel: We'll produce a CSV with the matrix: config, quant, batch/max_wait, p50/p95 latency, throughput (tokens/s), estimated cost per 1M tokens (hosted vs dedicated).
[08:46] Emily Rogers: For the dedicated option, what commitment level moves the needle materially? Our procurement would consider a 12 month reserved capacity if the numbers are compelling.
[08:55] Avery Chen: Typically a 3–6 node reserved contract with predictable throughput will move pricing about 30–45% lower than hosted list, depending on model and utilization. We'll show committed vs spot differ in the report.
[09:08] Nina Lowe: Are there minimums for Dedicated?
[09:11] Avery Chen: We'll include tiering. We can also show a hybrid where interactive routes stay on hosted and heavy batch inference goes to dedicated.
[09:20] 
[18:02] (mid-call — technical clarifications)
[18:02] Marcus Patel: One caveat on token accounting — your tokenizer may split certain unicode or domain tokens in ways that change counts vs naive assumptions. Send sample raw text so we can tokenize client-side and produce exact token histograms.
[18:15] Diego Martinez: We'll export raw requests and minimal PII redaction.
[18:20] Marcus Patel: Great. Also, if you have multi-turn chat state, we need to know your retention policy (how many turns you keep). That impacts total token generation.
[18:29] Emily Rogers: We keep last 6 turns typically, sometimes the whole session for premium customers. We'll annotate that in the sample.
[18:35] Marcus Patel: Perfect. For the bench harness we'll emulate that retention to get realistic per-request token counts.
[18:40] 
[28:05] (pricing & procurement)
[28:05] Avery Chen: I'll send the initial pricing sheet with three lanes: hosted pay-as-you-go, reserved dedicated (12/36 month), and private (VPC/on-prem) with professional services. We'll also include sample contract terms for pilot.
[28:18] Emily Rogers: Procurement would like to see data residency options; most of our EU customers must stay in eu-west-1.
[28:25] Avery Chen: We have EU regions; we'll call out region pricing and any egress implications.
[28:31] Diego Martinez: For the audit logs, can you include sample output format? Our SRE wants to ingest into Splunk.
[28:37] Marcus Patel: Yep, we'll attach a sample log and a small ingestion guide.
[28:43] Nina Lowe: One more question on regressions — how will Redwood handle a quality regression discovered after roll-in? Do you provide model rollback and A/B?
[28:52] Marcus Patel: Yes. We support model version pinning, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to previous model if quality alerts trigger. We'll include the runbook.
[28:59] 
[38:10] (recap and concrete closing)
[38:10] Avery Chen: Quick recap: SE will run the 1M token baseline matrix (int8/4-bit x low-latency/high-throughput batches) and produce per-1M token costs and latencies. We'll include both hosted and dedicated modeled pricing. You'll share 5k redacted queries, tokenizer histogram, and eval set. We'll send pricing, SOC2/ISO, and pilot contract.
[38:32] Emily Rogers: That matches our expectations. If you can get the baseline to us by end of next week that's great.
[38:39] Marcus Patel: We'll target the baseline report by 2026-02-21.
[38:43] Avery Chen: I'll send the pricing and security bundle by 2026-02-17.
[38:47] Diego Martinez: We'll aim to get the sample set to you by 2026-02-18.
[38:51] Nina Lowe: And we'll schedule the benchmark kickoff — 60 minutes — for early next week.
[38:57] Avery Chen: Great. Anything else before we wrap?
[39:01] Emily Rogers: One small ask — can the report include a sensitivity chart that shows cost per 1M tokens vs batch latency from 5ms to 200ms? That helps procurement see tradeoffs.
[39:11] Marcus Patel: Yes we'll include that. We'll also add a caching sensitivity axis.
[39:18] Avery Chen: Awesome. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with attachments and calendar invites.
[39:24] (call ends)
